name: Children’s Railway
description: A 760 mm narrow-gauge line of about 11 km through the Buda hills between Széchenyi-hegy and Hűvösvölgy, opened in stages from 1948 to 1950. Children aged roughly 10 to 14 perform most station and train duties under adult supervision, a practice recognised by Guinness World Records in 2015.

children.text: The Children's Railway, in Hungarian Gyermekvasút, runs through the Buda hills between Széchenyi-hegy and Hűvösvölgy. Wikipedia gives the length as 11.2 km (its history text says 11.7 km), the gauge as 760 mm, the maximum speed as 20 km/h and the journey time as about 40 to 45 minutes. The two termini are about 235 metres apart in elevation. It is single-track and not electrified.

Children aged 10 to 14 operate all posts except the train driver, under adult supervision. We Love Budapest describes the roles as ticket inspectors, brakemen, cashiers, announcers and platform attendants. In 2015 Guinness World Records recognised it as the longest railway on which commercial traffic services are run by children.

The railway was started in 1948. MÁV decided in 1947 to build a children's railway, and Wikipedia says construction began on 11 April 1948 and the first section, from Széchenyi-hegy to Előre, now Virágvölgy, opened on 31 July 1948. The line reached Szépjuhászné about a year later and Hűvösvölgy on 20 August 1950. It was originally called the Pioneer Railway, Úttörővasút, and it closed during the 1956 revolution without damage and reopened on 3 February 1957.

The stops make a useful route through the hills. Counting the termini, the line stops at Hűvösvölgy, Hárs-hegy, Szépjuhászné, János-hegy, Virágvölgy, Csillebérc, Normafa and Széchenyi-hegy. A 198-metre tunnel lies just before Hárs-hegy. The station building at Hűvösvölgy houses a Children's Railway Museum, and at Széchenyi-hegy you can change to the Cogwheel Railway. Several stops are near other Buda hills sights, including the chairlift at János-hegy and the Normafa meadow.
Good to know
Timetables and tickets are on the official site, gyermekvasut.hu, which We Love Budapest says has English pages; check it for current opening times and the season.
At Széchenyi-hegy you can transfer to the Cogwheel Railway, and the Zugliget chairlift is near the János-hegy and Virágvölgy stops.
Vadaspark is a timetabled stop for the Wildlife Park, but We Love Budapest says it is served only for groups that request it in advance.

historyIntro: The Children's Railway in the Buda Hills is a real narrow-gauge railway in which almost every job except driving the train is done by children.

children.text: Construction began on 11 April 1948. The first section opened on 31 July 1948 and the last on 20 August 1950, so the line is dated 1948–1950. It was originally called the Úttörővasút, the Pioneer Railway, a name tied to the communist-era youth organisation. Today its official designation is MÁV Zrt. Széchenyi-hegy Gyermekvasút, the Children's Railway.

historySections.heading: A working line staffed by children

children.text: The 760-millimetre narrow-gauge line runs through the Buda Hills between Széchenyihegy and Hűvösvölgy, a distance of roughly eleven kilometres (the sources give 11.2 and 11.7). Apart from the train driver, the posts are run by children aged 10 to 14 under adult supervision.

name: Normafa
description: A meadow and plateau in the Buda hills, named after a beech tree struck by lightning in 1927, with a view over the city. It has been used for walking and winter sport for well over a century, and a phased renovation since the mid-2010s has added paths, a playground and visitor facilities.

children.text: Normafa is a recreation area in the Buda hills, in Svábhegy in Budapest's 12th district, and Wikipedia gives its summit as 477 metres. A long, narrow plateau connects Svábhegy and János Hill. The site is known for panoramic views, and the open meadow looks out over the capital.

The name comes from a beech tree. Older Swabian residents called it Viharbükk, the storm beech, and according to legend it sprouted when King Matthias was born, and some believe the king napped in its shade. The hegyvidek.hu page says that in 1840 the actress Róza Schodelné Klein sang an aria from Bellini's Norma under the tree because its appearance recalled a scene from the opera, and the name then spread to the meadow. Lightning felled the tree in 1927, and a plaque commemorating it was put up in 1967.

Svábhegy has attracted hikers since the 17th century. The cogwheel railway opened in 1874 and was extended to Széchenyi-hegy in 1890. Skiing is recorded from 1895, a toboggan run was built before the First World War, and two ski jumps, one small and one large, were built in the 1920s; both are now gone. The first electric ski lift opened on Kis-Normafa in 1971 and has also been demolished.

A multi-year improvement project began to renew the area. By November 2015 its first phase had repaved the main path to János Hill, added benches and rubbish bins and upgraded the playground on Anna Meadow. A February 2020 article described a further redevelopment with a new car park and visitor centre, and reported that kiosks selling strudel and snacks were set to move. Plans may have progressed since then, so treat current facilities as something to check locally.
Good to know
We Love Budapest says bus 21 from Széll Kálmán tér goes to the Normafa stop; BKK also names bus 21 or 211 for the walk to the Zugliget chairlift's upper station.
The Children's Railway has a Normafa stop, and the Zugliget chairlift's upper station is a 20 to 30 minute walk away through the forest.
The area is used for walking, running, cycling, sledging in winter and cross-country skiing; check the district's site for current conditions and facilities.

historyIntro: Normafa's story combines a famous tree, over a century of hiking and winter sport, and recent redevelopment. The name itself is tied to a beech that lightning felled in 1927.

children.text: Normafa is named after a beech tree on Svábhegy. Older Swabian residents called it Viharbükk, the storm beech. According to the hegyvidek.hu page, the actress Róza Schodelné Klein sang an aria from Bellini's Norma under the tree in 1840 because its appearance recalled a scene from the opera, and the name then spread to the surrounding meadow. A We Love Budapest article says the name was linked to Norma after 1840, and Wikipedia calls the tree allegedly a beech planted by King Matthias Corvinus. Lightning felled the tree in 1927 and a plaque commemorating it was erected in 1967.

Svábhegy has attracted hikers since the 17th century, first for its hunting grounds and then for the pilgrimage site at Zugliget. The cogwheel railway opened in 1874 and was extended to Széchenyi-hegy in 1890. Skiing is recorded from 1895, a toboggan run built before the First World War hosted sledding competitions, and car races were held on Svábhegy by 1920. Two ski jumps, one small and one large, were built in the 1920s and hosted domestic and international competitions. The district's page says the flourishing sporting life was halted by the Second World War but soon revived. The first electric ski lift opened on Kis-Normafa in 1971; it, like the jumps, has been demolished.

The Hotel Olimpia, opened in 1972 on the Normafa plateau, was later demolished, and the Eötvös Loránd Park now occupies its site. A multi-year improvement project by the local government completed its first phase by November 2015, including repaving the main path to János Hill and upgrading the playground on Anna Meadow. In February 2020 We Love Budapest reported that a new car park and visitor centre were planned, with the Eötvös Loránd Park on the site of the neglected Olympia Hotel under way. These reports are from different dates, so check what has been completed.

According to local legend, the beech that gave Normafa its name sprouted when King Matthias was born, and some people believe the king once napped in its shade. Wikipedia words the tradition differently, as a beech allegedly planted by Matthias Corvinus in the 15th century.
These are traditions recounted on the sources named here, and no document is cited for either version.

name: Bartók Béla Boulevard
description: A long Buda road climbing gently from the Gellért area through Móricz Zsigmond körtér towards the Feneketlen-tó lake, now lined with cafés, galleries and bookshops. It has carried several names since the 1870s and has been called Bartók Béla út since 1945.

children.text: Bartók Béla út is a main road in Budapest's 11th district, Újbuda. According to the Hungarian Wikipedia article on the street, it runs for about 2.96 kilometres between Szent Gellért tér and Vasút utca, crossing Móricz Zsigmond körtér and Kosztolányi Dezső tér on the way. It is one of the busiest radial roads of southern Buda. For visitors the interesting stretch is the one that rises gently from the Hotel Gellért area towards the Feneketlen-tó, the Bottomless Lake.

The street was not always named after the composer. The first section, from Szent Gellért tér to Móricz Zsigmond körtér, was called Fehérvári út from 1874 to 1920, and the outer section towards Kelenföld railway station was Átlós út from 1890 to 1920. In 1920 both were renamed Horthy Miklós út. The name Bartók Béla út dates from 1945. Building along the road followed the 1913 zoning plan, and it is lined mostly with residential blocks of three to five storeys.

Transport shaped the street early. A tram first ran along it in 1898, linking Kelenföld railway station with Móricz Zsigmond körtér, and in 1899 the Dél-Budai HÉV suburban railway began running from Szent Gellért tér along Fehérvári út. The tram depot at Kelenföld has operated since 1912. The same article notes that cobblestones were replaced with asphalt in 2002 and 2003, and that the tram track between Szent Gellért tér and Móricz Zsigmond körtér was renovated in 2016.

In recent years the road has been described as a success story. A We Love Budapest walk published in January 2022 calls it once neglected but now full of cafés, restaurants, galleries and boutiques. It mentions the Hadik café, an old literary café where Frigyes Karinthy, Dezső Kosztolányi and Tibor Déry met, and Pagony, described as Hungary's largest children's bookstore. It also lists small galleries including Godot Gallery, Zsófi Faur Gallery, Artphoto Gallery and Dokubrom, which shows archive photographs edited by the Fortepan team.

The walk in that article ends at the Feneketlen-tó, where it lists the Figaró Magic Shop, run by the Szabó family since 1969. By the lake's playground it also notes a statue of a teddy bear, Mackó, by the sculptor László Molnár, there since 1961. The Hungarian Wikipedia article adds that a programme called Bartók-negyed, started after the M4 metro opened and bus traffic fell, strengthened the cultural role of the stretch between Móricz Zsigmond körtér and Szent Gellért tér.
Good to know
Szent Gellért tér at the Danube end is the natural starting point; the We Love Budapest walk begins at Fővám tér on the Pest side and crosses Liberty Bridge.
The Feneketlen-tó park at the far end of the walk has tennis courts, a running track and an outdoor gym.
Cafés, shops and galleries change often, so check each venue's own page for current opening times before planning a stop.
Trams run along the street; check the BKK journey planner for current routes and service.

historyIntro: Bartók Béla út grew from a Buda road that carried two different names before the First World War and was renamed twice more. Rail and tram lines reached it in the 1890s, long before the cafés and galleries of today.

historySections.heading: Fehérvári út and Átlós út, 1874 to 1920

children.text: According to the Hungarian Wikipedia article on the street, the section from Szent Gellért tér to Móricz Zsigmond körtér was called Fehérvári út from 1874 to 1920. The section from the körtér to Vasút utca, near Kelenföld railway station, was called Átlós út, but only from 1890 to 1920. Both names describe a road leading out of Buda towards the south and west rather than a boulevard of the kind it became. Building along the route followed the zoning plan of 1913, which set the pattern of the residential blocks of three to five storeys that line most of it today.

historySections.heading: Rails and trams reach the road, 1898 to 1942

children.text: Transport arrived early. A tram ran along the street for the first time in 1898, linking Kelenföld railway station with Móricz Zsigmond körtér. In 1899 the Dél-Budai HÉV suburban railway started from Szent Gellért tér along Fehérvári út, splitting after Albertfalva into one branch for Budaörs and Törökbálint and another for Budafok and Nagytétény. Trams 19 and 49 began service in 1910, and the Kelenföld tram depot has operated since 1912. In 1942 the HÉV was shortened to the building known as the Gomba at the körtér, which was completed that year.

historySections.heading: New names and recent renewal, 1920 to today

children.text: In 1920 the Council of Public Works renamed Fehérvári út and its continuation, Átlós út, as Horthy Miklós út. In 1945 the road was renamed Bartók Béla út. The cobblestones were replaced with asphalt in 2002 and 2003, the reconstruction reached Kelenföld railway station in 2005, and the tram track between Szent Gellért tér and Móricz Zsigmond körtér was renovated in 2016. After the M4 metro opened and bus traffic fell, the Bartók-negyed programme strengthened the cultural role of the stretch between the körtér and Szent Gellért tér, the same stretch that now holds many of the street's cafés and galleries.

stories.title: The composer's will and the street's name

children.text: The Hungarian Wikipedia article suggests that the choice of Bartók's name in 1945 may have been symbolic. It notes that the composer opposed Nazi-aligned ideas and emigrated from Hungary in 1940, and that in his 1940 will he stated that his name should not be used for public spaces in Hungary while places in Budapest were named after Hitler and Mussolini.
